name: The Chinkapin Oak of Wurster Park

location.address: Wurster Park, 525 W Madison St, Ann Arbor, MI 48103 (just into the woods at the park's southwest corner)

official_register.name: Michigan Big Tree Register (Michigan Botanical Society)

access: Free, public city park of 5.5 acres. The oak is near the south-west corner, just inside the woods. Dogs on leash.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 5.5 metres round, the thickest of any tree on Ann Arbor's champion list. It stands just inside the woods at the south-west corner of Wurster Park.
transport: Wurster Park is at 525 W Madison St in the Old West Side; bus routes not checked.
story:
The largest chinkapin oak in Michigan stands a few steps into a neighbourhood wood, in a park of five and a half acres. The city of Ann Arbor says so on the park's own page, and goes further. By girth, this is the biggest tree of any species in town.

The city's Champion Tree Map has it at 549 centimetres round and 35.7 metres tall, with 359.5 points, the score that decides who holds a title. The Michigan Big Tree Register measured the same trunk in 2016 at 215 inches round, almost exactly the city's figure, but put the height at 110 feet against the city's 117 and the crown at 120 feet against 106. Four years apart, and not in agreement, which is worth knowing before anyone quotes you a number.

A local blog says this is the tree shown in Wikipedia's article on the species. We have not been able to confirm that. The park also holds a champion black oak, which we have not located.

Nobody has published an age for this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.

name: The Bur Oak of West Park

location.address: West Park, Ann Arbor, MI, in the middle of the park east of the bandshell

access: Free, public city park near downtown.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 37 metres across and wider than the tree is tall, over a trunk 5.2 metres round. It stands in the middle of West Park, east of the bandshell.
transport: West Park is close to downtown Ann Arbor; bus routes not checked.
story:
This oak is wider than it is tall, by about ten metres. Ann Arbor's Champion Tree Map gives it a crown of 121 feet on a height of 87.2 feet, which makes it more shade than height.

The trunk measures 520 centimetres round. On the city's points system that comes to 322.2, enough to make it the champion of its species in town since 2020. The city's largest tree by girth, the chinkapin oak in Wurster Park, a little over a kilometre south, is only 29 centimetres thicker round.

The map is the only source we have for this tree, and it comes from the city, which owns the ground and does the measuring. The same map says a champion reigns for two years after verification, and we have found no independent report on this oak since 2020, so treat its title as the last one on record.

You will find it in the middle of the park, east of the bandshell, about 120 metres from the red oak at the Miller Avenue entrance. Nobody has published its age. If you know it, tell us.

name: The Red Oak of West Park

location.address: West Park, Ann Arbor, MI, at the Miller Ave entrance

access: Free, public city park near downtown.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 3.7 metres round, and by where it stands. It is the big red oak at the Miller Avenue entrance to West Park, the first champion you reach from that side.
transport: West Park is close to downtown Ann Arbor, at the Miller Ave entrance; bus routes not checked.
story:
Ann Arbor keeps score of its trees, and this one came in at 251.9 points. That made it the city's champion northern red oak in 2020, with a trunk 374 centimetres round, a height of 25.1 metres and a crown of 89 feet, all from the city's Champion Tree Map.

It is the junior partner in West Park. The bur oak about 120 metres away in the middle of the park scored 322.2, and if you have only ten minutes you should go and stand under that one first. But you will walk past this tree to get there if you come in from Miller Avenue, which is the best reason to stop and look up.

Red oaks carry a risk that the city's forestry office takes seriously enough to give a section of its web page to, the fungal disease called oak wilt. The map is our only source for this tree and we have found no report on it since 2020, so if you pass it and it is gone or ailing, we want to know.

Nobody has published an age for it either. If you know it, tell us.
